headline: Sixty thousand people cross into Ceuta in one day

sources.title: Migrant deaths in Ceuta rise to 72 after border surge from Morocco

chunks.text: About 60,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on Thursday, July 30. Ceuta is a small Spanish [[enclave]] on the north coast of Africa, with about 83,000 [[residents]]. Most of those who came {{set out}} from beaches near the Moroccan town of Fnideq and swam around the end of a stone [[breakwater]] that stretches into the sea. No city that size can {{take in}} that many people [[in a single day]]. At least 72 of them died, most of them [[drowned]] or were [[crushed]] against the rocks, and officials say the number may still {{go up}}.

verbs.wrong: To travel in a large group
verbs.why: Hikers set out at dawn to reach a summit, and sailors set out from port before a storm arrives. Most of the migrants set out from beaches near the Moroccan town of Fnideq before swimming toward Ceuta.

verbs.wrong: To count people as they arrive
verbs.why: A shelter takes in families after a fire, and a small town can take in visitors during a festival. Ceuta, a city of only 83,000 residents, could never take in 60,000 people arriving in a single day.
Grocery prices go up every summer, and a fever can go up quickly overnight. Spanish officials warned that the death toll from the crossing could still go up in the days that followed.

chunks.text: The reason [[lies partly in]] a court case. In June, Spain's Supreme Court {{handed down}} a [[ruling]] that stopped the government from returning people who arrive by sea without first hearing their case. Word {{got around}} on Moroccan social media that anyone who reached Ceuta by water could no longer be {{sent back}} the same day. That was [[not quite]] what the court had said, but thousands believed it. For years Moroccan police had {{held back}} crowds at the border fences, and [[youth unemployment]] in Morocco sits near 37 percent.

verbs.wrong: To send a case to a lower court
verbs.why: A judge hands down a sentence in open court, and a panel hands down a verdict after weeks of hearings. In June, Spain's Supreme Court handed down a ruling about people who arrive by sea.

verbs.correct: To become known by many people
verbs.wrong: To be posted by a government office
verbs.why: A rumor gets around a small office within a day, and gossip gets around a school before lunch. Word got around on Moroccan social media that people who reached Ceuta by water could no longer be forced to leave the same day.

verbs.correct: To make someone return to their own country
verbs.wrong: To record someone's name at the border
verbs.why: Airlines send back passengers without a valid visa, and a country can send back people who cross the border illegally. The rumor claimed that arriving in Ceuta by water would stop officials from sending migrants back the same day.

verbs.correct: To stop people from moving forward
verbs.wrong: To keep a road closed at night
verbs.why: Security holds back fans until a stadium gate opens, and a thin line of officers can hold back a large crowd. For years, Moroccan police held back crowds at the border fences near Ceuta.

chunks.text: Spain's answer came quickly. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez flew to Ceuta on Friday and called the crossing a [[violation of]] Spanish [[sovereignty]]. His government {{ruled out}} declaring a national [[emergency]], but it sent extra police, and on Saturday workers {{put up}} a floating [[barrier]] 500 meters long across the sea border. On the other side, Moroccan [[riot police]] used [[tear gas]] and [[water cannon]] to clear people from the gates. Twenty-two European countries {{called for}} emergency talks, Italy suspended passport-free travel with Spain, and France [[tightened]] its own border.

verbs.why: A company can rule out layoffs before a hard quarter, and a coach might rule out a risky play. Spain's government ruled out declaring a national emergency, though it still sent extra police to Ceuta.

verbs.correct: To build something as a barrier
verbs.why: Workers put up a fence around a construction site, and a city puts up flood walls before a storm. Spanish workers put up a floating barrier 500 meters long across the sea border in just one day.

verbs.wrong: To agree to a plan without a vote
verbs.why: Doctors call for stricter safety rules, and a mayor can call for calm after a difficult week. Twenty-two European countries called for emergency talks once news of the mass crossing spread.

chunks.text: By Saturday morning the [[flow]] had [[reversed]]. More than 48,000 people were back in Morocco within two days, and Spain's interior minister described Morocco as a partner [[rather than]] a threat. The crossings {{died down}} almost as fast as they had begun. The questions they {{brought up}} are much harder to settle. The Civil Guard is still {{going through}} [[fingerprints]] and DNA to [[identify]] the dead, more than a thousand people needed [[medical treatment]], and the city [[morgue]] has received 88 bodies, some of them from earlier attempts in the same two weeks. The new barrier covers 500 meters of the only [[land border]] between the European Union and Africa.

verbs.wrong: To stop for one night only
verbs.why: Loud applause dies down after a few minutes, and anger between old friends can die down in a week. The crossings into Ceuta died down almost as fast as they had begun.

A child brings up an old promise at dinner, and a coworker can bring up a topic nobody wants to discuss. The mass crossing brought up hard questions about the border that will take much longer to answer.

verbs.correct: To examine things one after another
verbs.wrong: To send evidence to another country
verbs.why: A detective goes through old case files, and a clerk goes through the mail every morning. The Civil Guard is still going through fingerprints and DNA to identify each of the dead.

mainIdea.s: About 60,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco within a single day, and at least 72 people died. Many wrongly believed a new court ruling meant they could not be sent back the same day.
mainIdea.why: About 60,000 people crossed in one day, and at least 72 died. Many wrongly believed a court ruling meant they could not be sent back the same day.

mainIdea.s: About 60,000 people reached Ceuta because Moroccan police opened the gates and guided them around the fences. Spain then built a sea barrier and sent most of the group back within two days.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Moroccan police spent years holding back crowds at the fences, and Spain sent most people back only after they had already arrived.

mainIdea.s: Spain and Morocco agreed months ago to reopen two crossing points near Ceuta for daily commuters. That agreement took effect this spring, well before the recent crossing made international news.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a separate agreement letting daily commuters use border crossings near Ceuta, not the mass crossing in July 2026.
